1. Introduction

   In industrial simulation packages, the BDF method with step size and order control is the most common integrator
for multibody systems [1]. The BDF method was first introduced as an implicit multistep method of order p = k for
ordinary differential equations by Curtiss and Hirschfelder [2]. BDF became famous for solving stiff differential equations
by the work of Gear [3]. In the present paper these BDF integrators are applied to multibody systems with large rotations
that are described without singularities by considering differential equations on manifolds with Lie group structure. The
corresponding equations of motion form a differential–algebraic equation (DAE) of index 3.
   Integrators for configuration spaces with Lie group structure have been considered by several authors. Crouch and
Grossmann [4] investigated the numerical integration of ordinary differential equations on manifolds with explicit
formulas for 3rd order multistep and Runge–Kutta methods by approximations directly in the Lie group G using several
combinations of the exponential map. To reduce the number of exponential maps, Munthe-Kaas [5,6] uses approximations
in the Lie algebra for Runge–Kutta methods on Lie groups. To obtain the high order in these Lie group formulations he
solves the kinematic equations on the Lie group by an ODE that acts on the corresponding Lie algebra and therefore
Lie brackets are involved. Celledoni, Marthinsen and Owren [7] tried to avoid Lie brackets and use a lower number of
exponentials than Crouch and Grossmann [4] for the Runge–Kutta methods. It depends on the problem whether less
exponential maps or less Lie brackets are computationally more efficient.
   The aim of the present paper is to use only one exponential per time step and to reduce the number of Lie brackets for
BDF Lie group integrators. Therefore ideas of Brüls and Cardona [8] are considered who have shown how to avoid time-
consuming re-parametrizations of the manifold in generalized-α time integration. They reformulate the generalized-α

  ∗ Corresponding author.
    E-mail addresses: victoria.wieloch@mathematik.uni-halle.de (V. Wieloch), martin.arnold@mathematik.uni-halle.de (M. Arnold).

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cam.2019.112517
0377-0427/© 2019 Published by Elsevier B.V.
2                            V. Wieloch and M. Arnold / Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics 387 (2021) 112517


method in terms of solution increments and combine linear updates of these increments with the exponential map to
update the configuration variables such that the Lie group structure of the (nonlinear) configuration space is respected. In
the present paper, an increment representation of BDF methods is used to get the BDF Lie group integrator BLieDF that has
a small number of Lie brackets and evaluates only one exponential per time step. This integrator is applied to constrained
mechanical systems that are described by Lie group differential–algebraic equations of index 3 for fixed step-sizes and
convergence with order p = k in all solution components is shown (for 2 ≤ k ≤ 4).
   In the unconstrained case, the application of multistep methods to differential equations on Lie groups has been
considered by Faltinsen, Marthinsen and Munthe-Kaas [9], who use strategies of Munthe-Kaas [5,6]. In the present paper,
this method is extended to Lie group DAEs of index 3 and denoted as Munthe-Kaas BDF Lie group integrator. In this
method, local coordinates and re-parametrizations of the manifold are evaluated before every time step to handle the
inherent nonlinearity of the Lie group formulations.
   In terms of computing time the novel approach BLieDF to BDF time integration on Lie groups is clearly superior to
existing multistep Lie group methods and has the potential to be implemented in industrial multibody system simulation
software.
   The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, the BDF methods for ordinary differential equations are introduced, as
well as some basics from Lie group theory. The BLieDF Lie group integrator for unconstrained and constrained mechanical
systems is explained in Section 3. The next section considers the Munthe-Kaas BDF Lie group integrator. Section 5
compares both approaches for 2 ≤ k ≤ 4. Afterwards the convergence with order p = k is proved for 2 ≤ k ≤ 4 for the
BLieDF integrator for unconstrained (Section 6.1) and constrained (Section 6.2) mechanical systems. The final section is
devoted to numerical tests for the Heavy top benchmark in the Lie group formulations R3 × SO(3) and SE(3).

2. Basic concepts

2.1. Increment representation of BDF

   BDF methods were originally proposed by Curtiss and Hirschfelder [2] for the time integration of first order ODEs. For
the application to second order ODEs

      q̈(t) = a(t , q(t), q̇(t))

with q : [t0 , te ] → RN , a : [t0 , te ] × RN × RN → RN , the equivalent first order system

      q̇(t) = v(t),                                                                                                              (1a)
       v̇(t) = a(t , q(t), v(t))                                                                                                 (1b)

with new variables v : [t0 , te ] → RN is considered. For fixed step size h, the time step tn → tn+1 = tn + h of a k-step BDF
discretization for the partitioned system (1) is given by
             k
       1∑
                 αi qn+1−i = vn+1 ,                                                                                              (2a)
       h
           i=0
             k
       1∑
                 αi vn+1−i = a(tn+1 , qn+1 , vn+1 )                                                                              (2b)
       h
           i=0

with known variables qn+1−i , vn+1−i , (i = 1, . . . , k). Eq. (2) defines solutions qn+1 and vn+1 . The method is initialized by
starting values qi ≈ q(ti ) and vi ≈ v(ti ), (i = 0, . . . , k − 1). The algorithmic parameters αi , (i = 0, 1, . . . , k) satisfy the
order conditions
      k                      k
      ∑                      ∑           (k − i)l
             αi = 0 and             αi              = l, (l = 1, . . . , k).                                                      (3)

In [10] it is shown, that method (2) for 1 ≤ k ≤ 6 has an order of convergence p = k and is zero-stable. The method is
A-stable for k ≤ 2 and A(α )-stable for 3 ≤ k ≤ 6.

   In the context of multibody system dynamics, the variables q, v and a represent position, velocity and acceleration
variables, respectively. The partitioned system (1) summarizes the kinematic equations (1a) and the dynamical equations
(1b). These dynamical equations result from the equilibrium conditions

      M(q(t))v̇(t) + g(t , q(t), v(t)) = 0                                                                                               (4)

for forces and moments by left multiplication with the inverse of the symmetric, positive definite mass matrix M(q) ∈
RN ×N :
      a(t , q(t), v(t)) := (M(q(t)))−1 (−g(t , q(t), v(t))).                                                                             (5)

The vector valued function g : [t0 , te ] × RN × RN → RN in the equilibrium conditions (4) denotes a force vector. As before,
the function a(t , q, v) represents the accelerations.
   The main interest of the present paper is in model equations in nonlinear configuration spaces with Lie group structure.
As seen in Section 2.2, the equilibrium conditions (4) and the dynamical equations (1b) keep their structure also in this
more general setting but the kinematic equations (1a) get a substantially more complex form. For this framework, it is
useful to rewrite the BDF discretization (2a) for the position coordinates q in the increment form
             k
        1∑
                  γi dqn+1−i = vn+1                                                                                                      (6)
        h
            i=1

with the one-step update qn+1 = qn + dqn and vectors

      dqn+1−i := qn+2−i − qn+1−i , (i = 2, . . . , k),

that are considered to be given in time step tn → tn+1 . Since
             k                                  k
        1∑                                 1∑
                  αi qn+1−i =                        γi dqn+1−i ,
        h                                  h
            i=0                                i=1

the new parameters are defined by

                  j=0

All in all, a k-step BDF integrator for (1) may be written in the form

For practical implementations, it is not efficient to calculate in (5) the inverse of matrix M(qn+1 ). Therefore Eq. (2b) is
multiplied with the mass matrix M(qn+1 ) resulting in the equivalent equation (7c).

2.2. Multibody systems: Configuration spaces with Lie group structure

    To describe a rigid body with large rotations in 3D spaces, a representation without singularities is not possible by
coordinates in a linear space. Therefore the position coordinates q in (1) must be coordinates of a nonlinear configuration
space with e.g. a Lie group structure.
    A Lie group G is a differentiable manifold with neutral element e, a differentiable group operation ◦ : G × G → G and a
differentiable inverse mapping q ↦ → q−1 (q ◦ q−1 = e). Following [11], the focus is on matrix Lie groups, which are defined
as subgroups of the general linear group GL(nG ). See [12] for a more general introduction to Lie group theory.
4                          V. Wieloch and M. Arnold / Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics 387 (2021) 112517


    The configuration of a multibody system at time t can be characterized by the position coordinates q(t) : [t0 , te ] →
G that describe position and orientation of all bodies in the system. As already discussed in [8,13], a continuously
differentiable function q(t) with q(t0 ) ∈ G will remain in a Lie group G if and only if its time derivative q̇(t) is in the
tangent space Tq G at the point q = q(t) : q̇(t) ∈ Tq(t) G, (t ≥ t0 ). The tangent space at the neutral element e defines the
Lie algebra g := Te G. As a linear space, it is isomorphic to a finite dimensional linear space RN with an invertible linear
mapping (˜ •) : RN → g, v ↦→ ṽ.
    The group structure of G makes it possible to represent the elements of Tq G at any q ∈ G by the elements ṽ of the
Lie algebra: The left translation Lq : G → G, y ↦ → Lq (y) := q ◦ y defines a bijection in G. Its derivative DLq (y) at y = e
represents the corresponding bijection between the tangent spaces g := Te G and Tq G, i.e.,

      Tq G = {DLq (e) · ṽ : ṽ ∈ g} = {DLq (e) · ṽ : v ∈ RN }.
In this framework, the kinematic equations are given by [8]

      q̇(t) = DLq (e) · ṽ(t)                                                                                                    (8)
with velocity coordinates v : [t0 , te ] → R .          N

    The exponential map exp : g → G maps the Lie algebra g to the Lie group G. In a neighbourhood of t = tm , the solution
of the kinematic equations (8) is given by

      q(t) = q(tm ) ◦ exp(Ω̃m (t − tm )), t ∈ R                                                                                  (9)
with Ω̃m (t) ∈ g solving the initial value problem
       ˙ m (t) = dexp
      Ω̃
                       −1
                             ṽ(t), Ω̃m (0) = 0                                                                                 (10)
                     −Ω̃ (t)m

a neighbourhood of Ω̃ = 0, this inverse is given by
                     ∑ Bk

and adkΩ̃ ṽ = adΩ̃ (adkΩ̃−1 ṽ) for k ≥ 1 and the Lie bracket [·, ·] : g × g → g which is a bilinear skew symmetric operation
on g, that would vanish when the Lie group G is replaced by a linear configuration space. The solution of (10) can be
calculated by the Magnus expansion [14] and approximated for t = tm + h by (see [15])
                                 h2            h3            h4 ...       h3                     4

h → 0. For a more detailed discussion on Lie groups in multibody dynamics see [13,15,16].

3. BLieDF

3.1. BLieDF integrator for unconstrained mechanical systems

   For unconstrained mechanical systems on Lie groups, the equation q̇ = v in (1) needs to be replaced by the kinematic
equations (8). With acceleration vector (5), the equations of motion become

               q̇(t) = DLq(t) (e) · ṽ(t),                                                                                     (13a)
      M(q(t))v̇(t) = −g(t , q(t), v(t))                                                                                        (13b)
                                                                                  N
with position coordinates q(t) ∈ G, velocity coordinates v(t) ∈ R , positive definite, symmetric mass matrix M(q(t)) and
force vector g(t , q(t), v(t)).
    Following the strategy of Brüls and Cardona [8], the traditional update of configuration variables in the kinematic
equations is substituted by updates of solution increments. Eq. (9) with m = n and t = tn+1 = tn + h, shows that
Ω̃n (h) ∈ g is the analogue to the solution increment dqn ∈ RN in (7a):

      q(tn+1 ) = q(tn ) ◦ exp Ω̃n (h) .
                                      (    )

Therefore the update of the configuration variables in time step tn → tn+1 is defined by

3.2. BLieDF integrator for constrained mechanical systems

    The BLieDF integrator (16) is applied to constrained mechanical systems. The equations of motion are given as
differential–algebraic equations in the index-3 formulation [8,16]

              q̇(t) = DLq(t) (e) · ṽ(t),                                                                                       (18a)
      M(q(t))v̇(t) = −g(t , q(t), v(t)) − B (q(t))λ(t),       T
                                                                                                                                (18b)
                  0 = Φ(q(t))                                                                                                   (18c)
                                                                                              N
with position coordinates q(t) ∈ G, velocity coordinates v(t) ∈ R , positive definite, symmetric mass matrix M(q(t)),
force vector g(t , q(t), v(t)), Lagrange multipliers λ(t) ∈ Rl , l ≤ N linearly independent holonomic constraints (18c) and
constraint gradients B(q(t)) with

      DΦ(q) · (DLq (e) · w̃) = B(q)w, (w ∈ RN ).                                                                                 (19)

To apply (16) to these equations, the holonomic constraint (18c) and the Lagrange multipliers λ need to be added. The
k-step BLieDF integrator (16) for constrained mechanical systems in the index-3 formulation (18) is for the time step
tn → tn+1 := tn + h defined by
                                                              ( (n) )
                                        qn+1 = qn ◦ exp ω̃0          ,                                                          (20a)

4. Munthe-Kaas BDF Lie group integrator

   Faltinsen, Marthinsen and Munthe-Kaas [9] consider linear multistep methods for first order ODEs on Lie groups. In
linear spaces, these methods coincide with their well known counterparts from classical ODE theory. In the application
of BDF to the partitioned system (13), they discretize the dynamical equations (13b) by
                          k
                  1∑
      M(qn+1 )                 αi vn+1−i = −g(tn+1 , qn+1 , vn+1 ),
                  h
                      i=0

5. Comparison of the two BDF Lie group integrators for 2 ≤ k ≤ 4

    The BDF Lie group integrators (16) and (22) address the nonlinear structure of the configuration space in different
                                                                                                                                      (n+1−i)
ways. In method (16) the increment BDF form (6) is directly applied, so that elements DLqn+1−i (e) ·ω̃0                for i = 1, . . . , k
from different tangent spaces Tqn+1−i G are used to update the configuration variables, see Fig. 1. The nonlinear structure
of the configuration space is considered by the correction term Lk in (16b).
    In contrast, method (22) is based on the classical BDF form (2) to solve for m = n the auxiliary ODE (10) that is defined
                                              (n−1)
in a linear space. The numerical solutions ω̃i       ∈ g with DLqn−1 (e) · ω̃(n
                                                                             i
                                                                                −1)
                                                                                    ∈ Tqn−1 G for i = 0, . . . , k − 1 of the previous
                                  (n)                        (n)
time step are transformed to ω̃i ∈ g with DLqn (e) · ω̃i ∈ Tqn G for i = 1, . . . , k, see Fig. 2. This re-parametrization
                                                      1
by BCHk -formulas and the approximations dexp−      k   reflect the nonlinearity of the configuration space and its Lie group
structure.
    The classical BDF discretizations in the velocity coordinates v (Eqs. (16c) and (22d)) are equivalent for both methods
(16) and (22), as well as their extension to constrained systems.
    For k = 2, both methods (16) and (22) can be written as

   For k > 2, the updates (16a), (22a) of the configuration variables and the equilibrium conditions (16c), (22d) are still

BLieDF with k = 4 may be implemented with the evaluation of one Lie bracket per time step, see (26). The numerical
effort of the Munthe-Kaas BDF Lie group method (27) is substantially larger since at least six Lie brackets have to be
                                                                                         (n)
evaluated and additional updates may be necessary in every Newton step since vn+1 and ω0 are involved (as for k = 3).

6. Convergence analysis

   The convergence of multistep methods for differential equations on manifolds is discussed in [9] and proves for
k ≤ 6 the convergence of Munthe-Kaas BDF Lie group integrators with order p = k (in the unconstrained case). In
the present section the convergence of fixed step size BLieDF for unconstrained systems is studied in Section 6.1 and for
the constrained case in Section 6.2. The convergence of Munthe-Kaas BDF Lie group integrators for constrained systems
may be studied in a similar way and will be discussed in full detail in future work. The convergence analysis for variable
step size implementations is substantially more complex and requires additional considerations, for example stability
conditions [18].

6.1. Convergence analysis for BLieDF: Unconstrained systems

   To prove the convergence of a multistep method in linear spaces, the method has to be consistent and zero-stable,
see [10]. For consistency, the local truncation error is defined by inserting the analytical solution into the numerical
10                             V. Wieloch and M. Arnold / Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics 387 (2021) 112517


method. For Eq. (16c) the local truncation errors lvn are given by

                      h

and correspond to the ones in linear spaces. Therefore, lvn = O(hk ), see [10]. Inserting the analytical solution Ωn+1−i (h) ≈

6.2. Convergence analysis for BLieDF: Constrained systems

   The proof of convergence for the BLieDF method for constrained equations of motion (20) is much more complex. The
holonomic constraint (18c) and the global errors eλn in the Lagrange multipliers λ must be considered (λ(tn ) = λn + eλn ).
The special structure of the constrained system results in additional higher order terms in all error estimates. Furthermore
the first k time steps must be examined separately, which was discussed in [22] in full detail and is omitted in the present
paper.
   For linear spaces Lötstedt and Petzold [23] showed the convergence of BDF for DAEs of Hessenberg form. For
the Lie group integrator, the convergence analysis starts with local error estimates (Theorem 2) and uses difference
approximations of hidden constraints to account for constraint equations and Lagrange multipliers (Theorem 4). In the
end, a coupled error recursion is obtained by which the convergence order p = k can be proven.

Theorem 2. The local truncation errors of the k-step BLieDF method (20) fulfil for k ≤ 4
                                                         ω
                                                         ln+1 − lωn 
                                                                     
      lω
       n = O (h ), ln = O (h ) and 
               k    v       k                                        = O(hk ).                                                            (38)
                                                              h      

  (a) As for unconstrained systems the local truncation errors lω    n are defined by (29) and with Lemma 1 the bound
      ∥lωn ∥ = O(hk ) can be shown. The local truncation errors lvn can be handled as in the unconstrained case and fulfil
      (38).
  (b) Let lωn be the local truncation error for the k-step BLieDF method (20) for the time step tn → tn+1 . The proof of
      Lemma 1 and (29) shows, that this error is given by lω
                                                           n = − k+1 h v (tn ) + h c(v(tn ), . . . , v
                                                                    1   k (k)     k                   (k−1)
                                                                                                            (tn )) + O(hk+1 ) (see [10,
         Table III.2.1]) with a function c, that consists of Lie brackets. Therefore the assertion follows, because of

see (36).              ■
   All in all the convergence of order p = k of the BLieDF integrator (20) for constrained systems (18c) can be proven
with the following theorem.

Theorem 4. If the global errors er , eω           λ

                                      r , er and er satisfy the technical assumption

        ∥eqr ∥ + ∥eωr ∥ ≤ C h, ∥evr ∥ + ∥eλr ∥ ≤ C .                                                                                                 (41)
for a constant C > 0, all r with t0 + rh ∈ [t0 , te ] and all h ∈ (0, h0 ] and the starting values q0 , . . . , q2k−1 , v0 , . . . , v2k−1 and

        2k−1                                    2k−1

then there are positive constants C , L and h0 independent of n and h, such that for all h ∈ (0, h0 ] and all n ≥ 0 with
t0 + nh ≤ te − h the following global error bounds hold
        ∥eqn ∥ + ∥evn ∥ + ∥eλn ∥ ≤ CeL(tn −t0 ) hk
and the BLieDF integrator (20) has the order of convergence p = k for 2 ≤ k ≤ 4.

Proof. The complete proof is given in report [24], see also the shorter version in the Appendix. The proof of this theorem
includes the following steps:
                                                              q
     (a) An error recursion for ∆h en , which follows directly from (40) is introduced.
     (b) An error estimate for ∥eλn+1 ∥ must be verified. Therefore the examination of the difference of the holonomic
         constraints (20d) at different time points is important to get an approximation of
                            k                                 k
                       1∑                            1∑
                                    αi evn+1−i =                       γi (evn+2−i − evn+1−i )
                       h                             h
                           i=0                            i=1

         which can be inserted into (39). The details are very technical and include e.g. the result of part (a), the derivatives
         of the holonomic constraints (20d), the local error estimates (38), as well as the technical assumptions (41).
         Furthermore this error estimate of ∥eλn+1 ∥ can only be proven for n ≥ 2k − 1 in this way. For the first k time
         steps (n < 2k) another strategy must be applied which was described in [22].
     (c) A coupled error recursion is obtained by combining parts (a), (b) and Eqs. (39) and (40) that allows to prove the
         order of convergence p = k, see also [13]. ■

7. Numerical tests

    The theoretical results should be verified in the numerical tests. Both integrators (20), (22a)–(22c), (23) are compared
in terms of order of convergence and efficiency. For the computing time the influence of implementation and Lie group
formulation should be examined. The numerical tests are done for the Heavy top benchmark, see Fig. 5, which is a rotating
spinning top with its tip fixed at the origin. The Lie group formulations R3 × SO(3) and SE(3) = R3 ⋉ SO(3) with the special
orthogonal group SO(3) = {R ∈ R3×3 : RT R = I3 , det R = 1} are examined [25]. At first the order of convergence was
tested for the Heavy top benchmark in the Lie group formulation R3 × SO(3) in Fig. 3. The absolute error at te of position
coordinate q (upper plots) and Lagrange multipliers λ (lower plots) over the step size h is plotted in double logarithmic
scale for the BLieDF integrator (left plots) and the Munthe-Kaas BDF Lie group integrator (right plots). The numerical test
illustrates an order of convergence of size p = k for 2 ≤ k ≤ 4 for both integrators for the solution components q and λ.
This corresponds to the theoretical examinations in Section 6.
    For the efficiency both integrators are tested for k = 2 at first. Section 5 shows that there is no difference between the
two integrators in this case. If implementation aspects have no influence on the computing time, then both integrators
should have the same behaviour. In Fig. 4 the absolute error at position coordinate q is plotted over the computing time
14                      V. Wieloch and M. Arnold / Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics 387 (2021) 112517




                                                               Fig. 5. Heavy top.




         Fig. 6. Efficiency of the integrators (24) and (25) for k = 3 in Heavy to benchmark (Left plot: R3 × SO(3). Right plot: SE(3) ).




         Fig. 7. Efficiency of the integrators (26) and (27) for k = 4 in Heavy to benchmark (Left plot: R3 × SO(3). Right plot: SE(3) ).




that is needed for all time steps without initialization for the Heavy top benchmark in the Lie group formulations R3 ×SO(3)
(left plots) and SE(3) (right plots). This test confirms, that there is no difference between the two integrators for k = 2.
    The three-step integrators (24) and (25) are tested in Fig. 6. The absolute error at position coordinate q is plotted over
the computing time that is needed for all time steps without the time for initialization for the Heavy top benchmark in
the Lie group formulations R3 × SO(3) (left plots) and SE(3) (right plots). To reach the same global error the BLieDF method
needs less computing time than the Munthe-Kaas BDF Lie group integrator regardless of which Lie group formulation is
used.
    Similar test results can be observed if the four-step integrators (26) and (27) are used, see Fig. 7.
    The numerical tests show that the BLieDF integrator was superior to the Munthe-Kaas BDF Lie group integrator
independent of the Lie group formulation and implementation aspects.

8. Conclusions

   The BLieDF integrator was introduced for unconstrained and constrained mechanical systems in Lie group formulations.
The equations of motion form ODEs or index-3 DAEs on Lie groups. In both cases, the convergence analysis proves an
                                 V. Wieloch and M. Arnold / Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics 387 (2021) 112517                                                 15


order of convergence of p = k for 2 ≤ k ≤ 4 for BLieDF. The novel integrator was compared with an earlier approach of
Faltinsen, Marthinsen and Munthe-Kaas and it was shown, that for 3 ≤ k ≤ 4 the BLieDF method is more efficient, since
it calculates less Lie brackets. For k = 2 both integrators are equivalent. The results were confirmed by numerical test
results for the Heavy top benchmark in the Lie group formulations R3 × SO(3) and SE(3).
